commentary:
Aquinas opens by locating this book within the larger project: having treated being in its various senses, he now turns to unity, which is convertible with being itself. He sorts the primary senses of 'one' into four: what is continuous by nature (most fully so when its motion is single and undivided, as with a straight or circular line); what is a complete whole possessing one form, especially when nature rather than glue or nails holds it together; what is numerically singular and so cannot be said of many things; and what is one in intelligibility, grasped by a single undivided act of understanding, as a species is grasped despite being realized differently in many individuals. All four, he insists, reduce to a single underlying note: indivisibility. Yet he draws a careful distinction between the things that are called one and what 'oneness' itself means - much as fire truly is an element without 'element' naming fire's own essence, so unity names an attribute that indivisible things have, not a separate nature.

Aquinas then follows Aristotle into unity's role as measure. Because the one is indivisible, it is the standard by which quantity of any kind becomes knowable - first and most properly the numerical unit, from which the notion of measure spreads analogously to length, weight, and even speed, always seeking the smallest, least-divisible standard so that nothing added or subtracted escapes notice. He extends this by analogy to knowledge and sense, which are called measures of things known and perceived, even though, properly speaking, it is the object that measures our cognition, not the reverse - a point aimed squarely against Protagoras's claim that man is the measure of all things.

Here Aquinas addresses whether unity is itself a self-standing substance, as the Pythagoreans and, following them, Plato supposed, or whether it is instead a property found in some underlying nature, as the early nature-philosophers assumed when they identified the ultimate 'one' with love, air, or the boundless. Aquinas sides decisively with the second view, tying it to a conclusion he had already established regarding substance: no universal can subsist on its own apart from the particulars it is said of, because a universal is by definition common to many, and what is common cannot also be a separate singular thing. Since being and unity are themselves the most universal predicates of all, extending to every category, they especially cannot name subsisting substances or constitute a genus in their own right. Aquinas develops this through Aristotle's illustrations from color, music, and speech: were all beings simply colors, they would form a number of colors and their 'one' would be some particular color, namely white; the same logic holds for tones and letters. The lesson generalizes to substance itself - in each category one must ask what the underlying one actually is, since 'being one' never suffices as a nature in its own right. Aquinas closes by clarifying the relation between unity and being: they are really the same subject, differing only in intelligibility, since unity adds nothing but the negation of division to being. He uses this occasion to correct Avicenna, who mistakenly treated being and unity as added accidental features of things, having been misled by the equivalent term 'one' that functions as a countable unit within the genus of quantity - a specialized sense distinct from the unity convertible with being itself.

Aquinas explains that unity and multitude are opposed most properly as the indivisible to the divisible, a relation he classifies among the contraries rather than among contradictories or correlatives, even though it carries a privative character, since 'one' is named from the negation of division found in its opposite. He notes an important asymmetry: multitude and divisibility are, in the order of our sense perception, more evident and so linguistically prior, which is why the one takes its very name and definition from what it negates - yet in the order of nature and reality, oneness remains prior, since indivisibility is presupposed by any division. From this basic opposition, Aquinas traces a family of related pairs. Sameness, likeness, and equality all cluster on the side of unity, while otherness, unlikeness, and inequality cluster on the side of multitude. He carefully distinguishes several senses of 'the same' - numerically identical, one in both form and matter, or one merely in the account of primary essence, as with equal lines. He is equally attentive to 'otherness': things differ absolutely when nothing about them is shared, but 'difference' proper is narrower still, requiring some underlying sameness - a shared genus or species - within which the differing items diverge. Difference, in other words, presupposes an identity that otherness as such does not. This sets up the book's central claim, which Aquinas signals here: that contrariety is itself a species of difference, indeed its most complete form, since contraries are precisely those things that differ to the greatest possible degree while still sharing a common genus.

Aquinas shows that wherever more and less can be found, a maximum must also be found, since an endless ascent is impossible; and because some things differ from others more than others do, there must be some pair that differs the most. This maximal difference he identifies with contrariety. He argues that things differing merely in genus cannot supply this maximum, since they are simply incomparable, admitting no scale of more or less; only things differing in species, where a genuine process of change runs from one extreme through intermediates to the other, allow for a true maximum - the two outermost termini of that process. Because the maximal and the complete coincide (nothing lies beyond either), contrariety is also perfect difference. From this Aquinas draws the corollary that a single thing can have only one contrary, since a single distance can have only two extremes, and he shows how this one definition underlies the four traditional descriptions of contraries offered by other philosophers - greatest difference, greatest difference within a genus, within the same recipient matter, and within the same science. He then turns to contrariety's root: privation and possession. Not every privation is a true contrary, only a 'perfect' one that reaches maximal distance from its corresponding possession - mere absence of color is not blackness's opposite to whiteness in the relevant sense. Aquinas carefully distinguishes contrariety from contradiction: contradiction is immediate and admits no middle term whatsoever, while contrariety, resting on privation attached to a determinate subject, characteristically does admit intermediates. Since generation and change move between contrary extremes, one member of every contrary pair must involve some privation, and ultimately all contrariety traces back to the primal opposition between the one and the many.

Aquinas takes up a genuine puzzle: if each thing has exactly one contrary, how can 'equal' seem opposed to both 'great' and 'small' at once, an arrangement that would seemingly violate that rule? He walks through the arguments on both sides. Some evidence suggests equal really does stand contrary to the great and small together, since we naturally ask 'whether' something is greater, smaller, or equal, and the word 'whether' properly signals opposition. Yet equal cannot be simply contrary to one of the pair alone, since there is no more reason to pair it with the great than the small, and it cannot be contrary to both together either, since that would mean one thing having two contraries, which is impossible; besides, equal functions as an intermediate between great and small, and contrariety, being maximal difference, admits no intermediate standing between itself and either extreme. Aquinas resolves this by denying that the opposition is contrariety at all: equal opposes the great and the small jointly as a privative negation, not as a contrary. It denies both excess and deficiency, but only within things naturally suited to have size at all - which is why the negation carries the sense of privation rather than a bare logical negation applicable to anything whatsoever. Because this joint denial falls upon one single, unified subject (quantity), it acquires its own name, 'equal,' unlike the analogous case of 'neither good nor bad,' which remains unnamed because goodness and badness admit no single unified underlying subject. This is also why equal serves as a genuine intermediate between the extremes, while some privative middles, lacking a single receptive nature, never received one manageable name at all.

Aquinas addresses a parallel puzzle about how the one is opposed to the many. If they were opposed without qualification, absurdities follow: since 'many' is opposed to 'few,' the one would have to count as few; and since two counts as 'many' in the sense that it is already a multiple, one would seem forced into the position of being a kind of plurality - which is impossible, since one is precisely what is not divided into a plurality. Aquinas untangles this by distinguishing two senses of 'many.' In one sense, it signifies an excessive plurality relative to some standard, opposed properly to 'few,' which signifies a deficient plurality; in this sense even 'much water,' a continuous quantity, can be called abundant without being 'many things.' In the other, stricter sense, 'many' simply means number as such, a plurality measured by the unit, and in this sense it is opposed only to the one, as the measured is opposed to its measure, not as a contrary. Two therefore counts as 'many' in this second, absolute sense, since it already constitutes a number, yet remains the very first and smallest instance of 'few,' since nothing is more minimal than two - one itself is not properly 'few' at all, only the ultimate measuring unit. On this basis Aquinas corrects Anaxagoras, who spoke of all things existing together, unbounded in both plurality and smallness: he ought instead to have said 'fewness,' since smallness (a continuous quantity) can regress infinitely by division, but fewness among discrete things cannot, having its natural floor at two. The one and the many, Aquinas concludes, are related as measure to measurable - a relative opposition, not a strict contrariety.

Aquinas explains why genuine intermediates must exist between contraries and how they are constituted. First, every intermediate belongs to the same genus as the extremes it stands between, since change from one thing to another - passing necessarily through whatever is intermediate - occurs only within a single genus; one cannot pass from color to shape except incidentally. Second, intermediates arise strictly between opposites of the contrary type: contradictories, admitting no middle at all, allow none; nor do non-reciprocal relatives such as knowledge and the knowable, since these do not share one genus. Only true contraries, like the great and the small, or colors ranging between white and black, properly admit a mean. Aquinas then works out the heart of the argument: intermediates are literally composed of the extremes. Since a genus is divided into contrary species by contrary differentiae - white and black, for instance, being distinguished as colors that respectively disperse or concentrate sight - those constitutive differentiae are themselves prior contraries. Any intermediate species, such as the colors lying between white and black, must likewise be composed from the genus and some differentiae, but these cannot simply be the same extreme differentiae (or every color would just be white or black); rather, they must be intermediate differentiae, sharing in the two primary contrary differentiae to varying, gradated degrees. Something that has more of one extreme's character and less of the other's is, in that very fact, compounded out of both extremes. Aquinas concludes that this holds throughout the whole hierarchy: every species within a genus, whether an extreme or an intermediate, ultimately traces back to and is composed from the primary contraries that first divide that genus.

Aquinas turns to what makes things differ in species, arguing that specific difference always presupposes an underlying sameness of genus: things other in species must nonetheless share one identical common nature, which is then differentiated in a non-accidental way in each - not merely that both are, say, animals, but that 'animality' itself is realized differently as equinity in the horse and humanity in the man. He explains carefully how genus relates to differentia: unlike matter, which is only part of the composite it underlies, genus is predicated of the whole species, being denominated from what is material in the thing, just as differentia is denominated from its formal principle, even though both genus and differentia, properly speaking, characterize the whole. Against Plato, who treated universals as separately subsisting realities, Aquinas insists that the common nature itself is diversified through its differentiae - 'animal' just is, in itself, differently realized as horse and as man. From this Aquinas concludes that specific difference simply is contrariety: since division of a genus can occur only through opposites, and neither contradictory nor privative nor non-mutual relative oppositions can divide a genus into coordinate species, only contrariety remains capable of doing so. A corollary follows: nothing is properly said to be the same or different in species with respect to its own genus, since genus, taken by itself, contains no differentiating contrariety at all - genus and differentia relate as an indeterminate, matter-like principle to something further needed to complete it, not as one species relates to a rival species within that same genus.

Aquinas confronts a natural difficulty: if contrariety is what makes things differ in species, why do male and female not constitute different species, given that masculine and feminine are genuinely contrary and belong to animal precisely as animal, not as an incidental attribute like paleness or darkness? He generalizes the puzzle - why does one contrariety, such as footed versus winged, produce specific difference, while another, such as pale versus dark, does not? His answer turns on the distinction between form and matter within a composite thing. Contrarieties located on the side of the formal principle, the very account or definition of a thing, do produce difference in species, since they diversify what a thing essentially is. Contrarieties located on the side of matter, however, do not, because matter individuates without altering the specific nature realized in it - a pale man and a dark man remain one species of man, since paleness belongs to this or that individual man materially considered, not to humanity as such. Aquinas applies this directly to sex: although male and female are proper, non-accidental differences of animal, they arise not from any difference in the animal's substantial form but from the disposition of its matter, namely the body, as shown by the fact that the very same seed becomes male or female depending on whether the vital heat acting upon it is strong or weak. Since one identical formal principle can issue in either outcome depending only on material conditions, sex cannot be a formal, species-determining difference, however genuinely it belongs to animal by nature rather than by accident.

Aquinas closes the book by showing that the perishable and the imperishable, unlike male and female, do differ in genus and not merely in species. His reasoning rests on the analysis of potency and privation developed earlier: incapacity is a form of privation, and privation grounds contrariety, so perishable and imperishable, opposed as a determinate capacity and its corresponding incapacity, are genuine contraries. But whereas contrarieties rooted in form and act (like the differentiae dividing a genus into species) produce merely specific difference, contrarieties rooted in potency - which pertains to matter, the principle from which genus itself is drawn - produce difference in genus. Perishability and imperishability, moreover, belong to their subjects necessarily and per se, not accidentally as paleness or darkness belong to a man; nothing can be perishable now and imperishable later, the way one man can be pale now and dark later, since what is accidental is by nature separable from its subject, while what is essentially corruptible cannot at some point cease being so without ceasing to be at all. Aquinas draws out the corollary Aristotle intends: this rules out the Platonic doctrine of separately subsisting Forms. If a sensible, perishable man and his supposed imperishable Form were truly the same in species, as the Platonists claimed, one man would simultaneously be both perishable and imperishable - an impossibility once perishability is recognized as a necessary, essential feature rather than an accident. Since things differing in genus are further apart than things merely differing in species, and since the corruptible and incorruptible differ in genus, no sensible thing and its purported eternal Form can share so much as one common species, let alone one identical individual nature.
